question.prompt: How many integers with four different digits are there between \(1{,}000\) and \(9{,}999\) such that the absolute value of the difference between the first digit and the last digit is \(2?\)

solutions.explanation:
Choose the first and last digits before filling the middle positions, since the difference condition concerns only the ends.

Every pair of digits differing by \(2\) has the form \(\{d,d+2\}\), where \(d=0,1,\ldots,7\). These eight pairs each have two orders, giving \(16\) ordered pairs. Exactly one order, \((0,2)\), is forbidden because a four-digit integer cannot begin with \(0\). Thus there are \(15\) allowed end-digit pairs; \((2,0)\) remains allowed.

After fixing an allowed pair, the hundreds digit can be any of the other \(8\) digits. The tens digit then has \(7\) choices, since all four digits must differ. Hence the total is
\[
15\cdot8\cdot7=\boxed{840}.
\]
Every valid integer has exactly one ordered end-digit pair and exactly one filling of its middle positions, so this counts every valid integer once. The answer is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
solutions.title: Choose the end digits first
